## [2026-11-19](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-19.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24540>)

A replicated factorial experiment tests five modern training ingredients jointly in small language models, separating average recipe effects from interactions and run noise. The 32-run study finds mostly additive loss gains within its tested settings, while showing why shared baselines, replication and explicit aliasing assumptions are needed before transferring isolated improvements into a combined recipe.

**Published:** 2026-11-18 · **First seen:** 2026-11-19T11:06:46.455+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Factorial Experiments, Training Recipes, Replication, Optimizer Evaluation

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2611.24540v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete five-page primary read, including design, implementation failures, statistics, results and limitations; actual p.3 Figure 1/Table 2 directly inspected. Sixteen resolution-V half-fraction configurations combine attention gating G, a Muon optimizer recipe M, sandwich normalization S, routed/shared experts E and a GatedDeltaNet hybrid H, repeated at two initialization/data-stream seeds (32 core runs). Each run trains about 300M FineWeb tokens with sequence length 1,024 and about 51.5M active parameters; MoE models instead have about 161.3M total parameters. Within-seed configurations share the data stream. Mean single-switch loss contrasts are E −0.0983, M −0.0506, H −0.0365, S −0.0194 and G +0.0018 nats. The largest pairwise alias contrast is MH/GSE +0.0122 nats; the repeated-run reference margin gives about 0.017 nats against the 0.02-nat practical bound. Five completed H-only runs and paired seed contrasts estimate run noise at 0.0036 nats, versus the sparse-effects estimate of 0.020. The all-five configuration is best only within the measured half-fraction. Original CL/LG NEW membership and dated RECENT November 19 header, sole-v1 receipt November 18 14:48:52 UTC, and official Wednesday-before-14:00 Eastern / Wednesday-20:00 announcement row support inferred November 19 01:00 UTC availability. Earliest completed team discovery is the pinned AI NEW receipt, not a request start. Exact-title/primary artifact searches found no verified earlier full study; this is a bounded chronology check, not proof of first-ever public disclosure.

**Limitations:** The half-fraction aliases each main effect with a four-way effect and each pair with a three-way effect; two-seed replication does not resolve these aliases. The independence/equal-variance noise interval is a reference under assumptions, since shared streams can correlate errors. MoE changes total capacity; gates reduce feed-forward width to match active parameters; Muon and the hybrid are bundled recipes rather than isolated primitives. Only one corpus, a small active model, short context and token-matched budgets are tested, without matched wall time, FLOPs, energy, downstream accuracy or long-context evaluation. Learning rates and final results use the same validation set; unmeasured combinations, independently tuned recipes and frontier scales may differ. No matching author code/checkpoint release was verified.

## [2026-11-17](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-17.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19419>)

A controlled study tests optimizer transfer from pretraining to short-horizon, teacher-probability distillation using four Qwen student–teacher pairs and fixed update budgets. Its evaluated matrix-structured recipes show no consistent advantage over AdamW or AdaGrad in teacher matching versus trainer time, giving practitioners a concrete protocol for rechecking optimizer choices in the distillation setting.

Qwen3 0.6B←1.7B, 4B←8B, 14B←32B and Qwen2.5 32B←72B share within-pair teacher/student tokenizer, 79,535 Nemotron reasoning traces, 1,006 validation examples, batch 144 and 1,683 optimizer updates. Training balances answer/reasoning region means equally using pure forward KL; validation averages assistant tokens, a distinct length weighting. BF16 FSDP2/FP32 gradient reduction uses 72 GB200 accelerators for Qwen3 and 144 for Qwen2.5; no weight decay, scheduler or warmup. Full-budget results use three seeds and descriptive mean±SD of per-seed best validation KL, plus matched-step trajectories. AdamW generally achieves lower KL; every completed structured recipe adds trainer time, while AdaGrad is slightly faster on larger pairs. Trainer time includes training, validation and improvement-triggered checkpoints, excluding loading/queue/export. The linked repository is the existing surrounding distillation framework, not a verified release of the paper-specific optimizer adapters: Appendix A says those experiments will be released. **Limitations:** Only four dense Qwen pairs, one reasoning corpus and a short three-epoch-like schedule; validation KL is teacher matching, not downstream capability. All-2D Muon applies its spectral update to embeddings/head as well as hidden matrices, differing from the standard hidden-only recipe. Hyperparameter pilots and validation-selected final configurations do not impose equal tuning budgets. Largest-pair SOAP has one 561-step run taking 4.31× paired AdamW trainer time and is excluded from full-budget summaries. Backend/routing/blocking controls change algorithmic recipes as well as systems behavior; no universal ranking, optimizer-kernel-only timing, causal explanation of transfer failure or independent reproduction is established. ### [Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17876>)

The updated Muon study adds norm-reset interventions and 3.4B-parameter runs to an earlier investigation of temporary weight decay. Swapping weight norms at the end of decay transfers much of the later loss benefit in the tested small models, while larger-model experiments show why early loss regressions should be assessed again at the final training budget. These controls strengthen a specific optimization diagnosis, rather than establishing a universal decay schedule.

**Limitations:** The new reset controls are individual matched comparisons and also immediately change model outputs, so they do not prove norms are the only causal state or that larger relative steps are always better. Most configurations, including 3.4B, are single-seed; the norm-control data differs across scales. Five 3.4B configurations use 32 H100 GPUs while the fixed-update transfers use B200s; transfer rules differ in duration and total shrinkage, and only two constant coefficients are sampled. Mean downstream gains do not imply every-task gains; earlier 405M/1.4B comparisons lack a clear advantage over constant decay. Gradual schedules can outperform the abrupt window. ## [2026-11-14](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-14.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [End-to-End 4-Bit Training](<https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/end-to-end-4-bit-training/>)

Thinking Machines describes a mixed-precision recipe that uses four-bit arithmetic for most expert-layer forward passes while retaining eight-bit backward computation. Re-quantizing saved forward tensors with stochastic rounding and compressing expert communications make low precision useful across pretraining and reinforcement learning. The authors report faster training on GB300 systems, alongside a small pretraining efficiency loss and limited public experimental detail.

**Published:** 2026-11-13 · **First seen:** 2026-11-14T11:01:01.560+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Mixed Precision, NVFP4, Stochastic Rounding, MoE

[Blog](<https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/end-to-end-4-bit-training/>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Small>)

**Evidence:** technical-report; full-text. Complete November 13 technical post inspected, including block-scaled transposes, stochastic re-quantization, communication formats and final recipe. Saved quantized forward weights/activations are dequantized, transposed and stochastically re-quantized to MXFP8 for backward GEMMs; 32-dimensional random Hadamard transforms and block-scaled S2F6 reduce combine payloads from 16 to 8.25 bits/value. Authors report 8% pretraining and 20% RL wall-clock speedups versus full MXFP8, with about 2% pretraining compute-efficiency loss. This is a delayed discovery within the 72-hour lookback: the post is dated November 13 and first retrieved today. Earlier Inkling 2 launch/card already disclosed native NVFP4 and the 68-hour run, but not these detailed numerical mechanisms; those older facts are not treated as new results.

**Limitations:** This is a GB300-specific author engineering report with in-house BBBK kernels, no controlled run table, seed intervals or independent reproduction. Four-bit applies to most expert forward computation, not the whole network or backward pass; the final one-sixth of layers uses MXFP8. Stochastic re-quantization targets the saved quantized forward value in expectation, not the original unquantized tensor or guaranteed unbiased total gradients. The 68-hour run combines many changes and does not isolate this recipe. Weights are public; a reproducible training/kernel implementation was not verified.

## [2026-11-11](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-11.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13545>)

This study traces slower low-learning-rate BF16 RL post-training to weight sticking, which persists even when training and rollout log-probabilities match exactly. Stochastically rounding FP32 shadow weights into the BF16 weights used by both backends matches FP16 reward trajectories across the tested math settings, without requiring FP16 loss scaling. It provides a targeted precision-recipe fix, with convergence measured in RL iterations and less reference-policy drift than simply increasing the BF16 learning rate.

**Published:** 2026-11-10 · **First seen:** 2026-11-11T11:05:34.533+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Mixed Precision, RLVR Stability, Stochastic Rounding

**Public availability:** 2026-11-11T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/new>) · [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13545v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. All 8 PDF pages read, including Sections 2-3 and Figures 1-7. Controlled DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B comparisons on MATH-1460 enforce bit-exact backend parity; mantissa-width and learning-rate sweeps support weight sticking as a contributor. Larger experiments use 14B distill models on MATH-1460/DAPO-Math-17k and Qwen3-30B-A3B on MATH-1460, with AIME 2024/2025 mean@32 evaluation. The simplest supported variant draws one stochastic weight realization after each optimizer step and reuses it in all forward passes until the next step, including synchronized rollout generation. The original November 10 receipt date is retained; first announcement is inferred from its original November 11 LG batch and official schedule.

**Limitations:** Convergence speed means iterations to reward/score, not a measured wall-clock speedup. BF16 often catches up on downstream AIME later, so this is not an across-the-board final-quality gain. Parity controls use 64 H100s and other experiments 64 B200s; seed confidence intervals are not reported. TorchInductor observations cover the old vLLM 0.12-0.17 versions tested, not current releases. Frontier agentic/MXFP8 remarks are preliminary. Stochastic rounding is an established technique; this contribution is the controlled RLVR diagnosis/application, not invention of stochastic rounding. No author implementation was verified.

### [Multi-Token Prediction Done Right (Soft-MTP)](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38331>)

Soft-MTP routes future-token heads toward the model’s aligned next-token distribution while retaining ordinary cross-entropy supervision on the shared output head. It recovers this distillation gradient from existing losses without extra full-vocabulary tensors, improving the tested training-quality and self-speculative-decoding trade-off.

A separate logits-aware distillation construction uses log1p/expm1 and a projected custom gradient to preserve small teacher–student differences instead of subtracting independently rounded probabilities. This second construction requires teacher logits, not only already-rounded target probabilities. The hard-target precision cliffs are approximately margin 5.5 in bfloat16, 16.6 in float32 and 36.7 in float64; casting up delays the cliff. Controlled grokking experiments include one-layer Transformers and two-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic. The principal modular-addition experiment uses a one-layer width-64 Transformer, modulus 31, a 50% training split and 10,000 full-batch AdamW epochs. Table 1 sweeps three precisions and three Adam epsilon values over five seeds; at float32 and epsilon 1e-8, the fixed formulation reports 100.0% mean test accuracy versus 94.3% for standard cross-entropy. The distillation diagnostic begins with a student identical to an already-correct modular-arithmetic teacher, uses temperature 4, 2,000 Adam steps and three seeds, and demonstrates drift from numerical cancellation rather than useful learning from a stronger teacher. Prior work already identified collapse/slingshot behavior and proposed mitigations; the contribution is the direct stable formulation and joint numerical/optimization analysis, not the first observation of all such failures. **Limitations:** Evidence is controlled small-model arithmetic/grokking and near-identical-network distillation, not a demonstrated improvement in ordinary large-scale LLM training or downstream language capability. The authors explicitly note that the extreme confidence and near-zero teacher–student gaps may be uncommon in standard large-scale regimes. Results across precisions and optimizer epsilon settings do not establish a universal accuracy gain or an optimizer-independent training guarantee. ## [2026-10-22](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-22.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29348>)

Controlled experiments show that a data-mixture schedule can help or hurt mid-training depending on when the learning rate decays, even when total compute and target-data tokens are fixed. Dense and mixture-of-experts experiments favor keeping the rate high after target data first appears and using a short final cooldown to lower target-domain validation loss, giving recipe designers a reason to tune the two schedules together.

**Published:** 2026-10-21 · **First seen:** 2026-10-22T10:07:41.810Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Data Mixtures, Learning Rate Schedules, Mid-training, Mixture of Experts

**Public availability:** 2026-10-22T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.29348v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Pinned v1 Sections 2–4 and relevant setup, repeat-run, data-schedule and cooldown appendices inspected. The study holds continuation compute and mid-training token budget fixed while varying the target-data fraction over time and the learning-rate schedule, across over 250 runs with a 630M dense model and a 2.99B-total-parameter MoE model (454M active non-embedding parameters plus embeddings). The dense model continues for 20.97152B tokens after 200B DCLM pretraining; the MoE main study uses 4B or 10B continuation tokens after 40B pretraining. FineMath is the principal target corpus, with code-data checks as well. Two-stage jumps and zero-then-linear ramps interact differently with constant learning rates and full- or matching-window decay: earlier mixing can help under full decay but lose its advantage under a constant rate. Across 19 tested cooldown sweeps, the best tested decay spans 10–40% of the mid-training window, rather than necessarily beginning when target data first appears. A ramp can have twice the mid-training window at the same target-token budget, so fractional cooldowns must also be compared in absolute steps. For example, the dense 25%-budget two-stage configuration reaches target validation cross-entropy 1.4275 with a 40% cooldown versus 1.4717 with constant learning rate and 1.4475 with decay over the matching mid-training range. These are configured-tokenizer loss units, not downstream accuracy. Selected configurations are repeated with three data-stream/order replicates sharing the same pretrained checkpoint; most sweeps have one run. Fresh optimizer state, no continuation warmup, and the within-family optimizer settings are held fixed. The original October 21 receipt (07:42:20 UTC) is retained. The paper appears in the original October 22 new-submission batch; October 22 00:00 UTC availability is inferred from that dated batch and the official Eastern-time announcement schedule. No earlier primary release was found in the bounded title/artifact search, which does not prove absence of one. The paper cites prior curriculum and schedule studies; the contribution is its controlled budget comparisons and recipe evidence, not the first observation that data and optimization interact.

**Limitations:** Evidence concerns target-domain validation loss at these model/data scales, not established downstream capability gains or a universal optimum. Pretraining loss can trade off against target loss. Only a few configurations have data-order repeats, and they share one pretrained checkpoint; close loss differences are not automatically statistically significant. The dense and MoE families have different tokenizers and optimizer details, so absolute losses are not directly comparable across families. The noisy-quadratic/SGD analysis explains the interaction under assumptions rather than proving the best schedule for Transformers. The 10–40% cooldown range is the best among tested choices, not a universal rule. No author implementation/project release was verified from the inspected primary source, and no independent reproduction was performed.

## [2026-10-09](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-09.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575>)

Elastic Expert Routing varies the number of active experts around the deployment budget during training, giving experts just beyond the usual cutoff occasional task-loss feedback. It improves the tested MoE models while retaining ordinary fixed top-k inference, providing a training intervention that preserves the serving architecture.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:03:31Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Mixture of Experts, Routing, Pretraining

**Public availability:** 2026-10-09T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11575>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. A 6–10 expert schedule centered on eight improves nine-task SFT averages by 0.84 points on OLMoE and 2.02 on Qwen3-30B-A3B; 1.42B-model pretraining improves its separate task average by 1.6 points. Original v1: 2026-10-08T09:31:19Z; October 9 new-submission batch verified.

**Limitations:** Matched expected expert FLOPs do not imply equal runtime: the preferred schedule costs about 3–5% more per SFT iteration. ## [2026-10-06](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-06.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LightMTP: Lightweight Latent Multi-Token Prediction](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06031>)

LightMTP adds a small auxiliary head that predicts the model's own future intermediate hidden states, using stopped-gradient targets from the same training pass alongside next-token prediction. The head is discarded at inference, offering an inexpensive way to encourage future-aware representations and improve some structured reasoning tasks without changing ordinary decoding.

**Published:** 2026-10-05 · **First seen:** 2026-10-06T10:03:05Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Pretraining, Multi-Token Prediction, Latent Targets

**Public availability:** 2026-10-06T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06031>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Experiments cover 286M–1.4B decoders and multiple seeds. Countdown accuracy rises from 46.4% for next-token training to 56.7% for a LightMTP variant; the main 24-layer heads add 0.3–0.9% parameters. Original submission: 2026-10-05T09:30:30Z; October 6's listing establishes the later 00:00Z public batch inside the main window.

**Limitations:** General-language aggregate results remain near the next-token baseline, and a linear token-prediction baseline scores higher on Countdown. Training budgets grow with head size and are not matched for tokens or compute; small parameter overhead is not zero training cost. Some headline GSM8K results use a relaxed matching metric. No author implementation was verified.

## [2026-09-30](../../../reports/2026/09/2026-09-30.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38149>)

LIFT trains language models to carry a latent state across generated tokens, using a teacher's next-token distributions to supervise this feedback channel while preserving parallel pretraining. Its controlled language-modeling and procedural-task gains suggest a way to improve learning efficiency and state tracking without expressing every intermediate computation as text.

**Limitations:** Only the smallest language-model scale has three training seeds; larger runs have one. ## [2026-09-29 — Landscape baseline](../../../landscape/2026-09-29.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534>)

Kimi K2 introduces MuonClip, which adds query/key weight clipping to Muon so that attention logits remain controlled during large-scale mixture-of-experts training. It is a practical optimization reference because it links a specific instability mechanism to an intervention used in a trillion-parameter training run.
